channel.title: Gaia's Secret Agents — Homeschool Nature Learning
channel.description: Outdoor learning, homeschool science and printable environmental activities for children.

item.title: Nature Walk Activity for Kids: A One-Minute Listening Mission
item.description: Try this simple outdoor listening activity together: stand still, listen for three different sounds and share what you noticed. An easy nature-study idea for a family walk or homeschool break. Save the prompt, then explore more screen-free nature activities and sound-map ideas from Gaia’s Secret Agents.

media:content.media:description: A kookaburra watches from a gum tree above a child and older adult, beside three steps for a family listening activity.

item.title: Backyard Nature Activity for Kids: A Tiny-World Safari
item.description: Go slow and spot more. Pause beside a plant, look for tiny movements and watch without disturbing wildlife. This simple backyard nature activity gives families and homeschoolers a reason to explore together. Save the three-step prompt, then visit Gaia’s Secret Agents for more mini nature missions.

media:content.media:description: A smiling parent and child observe a snail on a leaf, with three steps for a tiny-world safari.

item.title: Backyard Nature Study for Kids: A Free 5-Day Wildlife Tracker
item.description: How can children spot changes in a backyard habitat? Check the same little shelter each day and record the weather, visitors and clues. Watch wildlife without touching or feeding it. Get the free two-page tracker with a parent, guardian or teacher email.

media:content.media:description: Sunlight falls on a bark shelter resting on a mossy stone. The headline asks who visits one tiny patch of garden.

item.title: Five-Minute Nature Walk for Kids: Find Three Signs of Wildlife
item.description: How can you spot wildlife if the animal has already gone? Look for three signs such as a feather, a track or a nibbled leaf. Notice where each clue lies and leave it undisturbed. Try the free five-minute Nature Detective mission.

media:content.media:description: A pale feather lies beside seeds and a nibbled gum leaf in sunlit leaf litter. Text invites families to find three signs.

item.title: Homeschool Nature Journal: Spot a Spiderweb After Rain
item.description: What can a child record on a damp day? Note the weather, sketch a web you can see from the path and leave it in place. The free two-page Nature Tracker has room for five days of observations. Get the tracker with a parent, guardian or teacher email.

media:content.media:description: Water beads along a web between gum leaves. The headline invites children to observe after rain.

item.title: Wildlife Observation for Kids: What to Record on a Quiet Day
item.description: What if no animal appears during a backyard watch? Note the date, weather and what you actually saw, even if the visitor count is zero. Return to the same patch tomorrow. Get the free five-day Nature Tracker with a parent, guardian or teacher email.

media:content.media:description: A fallen leaf rests beside a purple stone on an empty mossy trail in morning light.

item.title: Outdoor Learning for Primary School: Compare Two Schoolyard Habitats
item.description: How can a class investigate biodiversity in 20 minutes? Compare a paved area with a garden edge, count visible signs of life from an agreed boundary and discuss which spot offered more shelter. Get the free eight-page Teacher Starter Pack with an adult email.

media:content.media:description: A paved schoolyard path divides flowering garden beds, with contrasting shade and sunlight.

item.title: Child-Led Nature Exploration: What Is the Grown-up’s Role in the Starter Kit?
item.description: Do I need to know the name of every plant? No. In the printable Starter Kit for ages 6–11, the child leads as the Agent. Grown-ups can ask what caught their eye and look up a discovery together afterwards. Explore the Starter Kit.

media:content.media:description: A child points out a curled fern frond while an adult kneels beside them in the bush.

item.title: Nature Colour Hunt for Kids: Find Five Colours Without Picking a Thing
item.description: How can we do a colour hunt without collecting leaves? Pick five colours, then point to examples in bark, stones, leaves or flowers. Allow 10–15 minutes and finish by comparing your most surprising finds. Try the nature colour hunt.

media:content.media:description: Cream, rusty orange and rose layers in a gum tree trunk catch the light.

item.title: Leaf detective activity for kids: what does a nibbled edge tell us?
item.description: What can a chewed leaf tell your child? Its missing edge is a clue that something may have fed there. Record the shape and weather, then check the same patch tomorrow. Get the free five-day Nature Tracker with a parent, guardian or teacher email.

media:content.media:description: A backlit green leaf has a curved notch in its edge.

item.title: Primary science observation sheet: help children back up a claim
item.description: How can I help a child explain a nature observation? Ask what they saw that supports their idea. The free Teacher Starter Pack includes a large-print evidence sheet and discussion prompts for ages 6–11. Get the pack with an adult email.

media:content.media:description: A brass magnifier frames a seedling in a flowering school garden.

item.title: Nature journal for kids: record the weather beside your wildlife clues
item.description: What else belongs in a wildlife record? Note the weather as well as visitors and clues, then compare what you notice over five days. The free Nature Tracker gives your family a place to record those observations. Get it with an adult email.

media:content.media:description: Rain droplets hang from a fern above a wet stone and fallen leaf.

item.title: Shorebird watching for kids: notice behaviour before learning names
item.description: Do we need to know a bird’s name to watch it? No. Keep your distance and spend five minutes tallying what one shorebird does, such as pecking, running or resting. Supervise children and avoid nesting birds. Try the free Shorebird Behaviour Watch.

media:content.media:description: A single small shorebird stands on wet sand beside turquoise surf.

item.title: Outdoor lesson planning for homeschool families with a reusable planning sheet
item.description: How can I plan a second outdoor lesson after the first one? Start with Operation: Hidden Habitat, then use the reusable planning sheet for your next investigation. Get the free eight-page Teacher Starter Pack with a parent, guardian or teacher email.

media:content.media:description: A blank clipboard and pencil sit on a bench beneath flowering gum branches.

item.title: Nature study for kids: make a field file about one garden insect
item.description: What can we write about an insect before we know its name? Sketch its shape, note its colour and record where you saw it and what it was doing. Leave it undisturbed and look up its name afterwards. Try the free One-Species Field File activity.

media:content.media:description: A red and black ladybird walks along a green leaf against a blue garden background.

item.title: Animal tracks for kids: read a footprint trail in soft ground
item.description: What can we record if the animal has already gone? Look at the direction of its tracks and sketch one print without disturbing it. Record the date and weather beside the sketch, then compare the same patch over five days. Get the free Nature Tracker with an adult email.

media:content.media:description: Bird tracks lead past a pale stone on a damp woodland path.

item.title: Rock pool activity for kids: count the kinds of life in one pool
item.description: How do we explore a rock pool without disturbing it? At low tide, watch from a safe spot with a grown-up and count the different kinds of life you can see. Leave rocks and animals where they are. Compare your count with a second pool. Try the free Rock-Pool Census.

media:content.media:description: A purple anemone and olive seaweed sit beneath the clear water of a coastal rock pool.

item.title: Screen-free primary science lesson without student logins
item.description: Does every child need an account to try an outdoor science lesson? No. A grown-up uses their email to access the free Teacher Starter Pack. Operation: Hidden Habitat takes about 20 minutes and includes a printable evidence sheet. Get the free teacher pack.

media:content.media:description: Four children walk with a grown-up towards a flowering tree.

item.title: Shade and heat experiment for kids: compare two spots on the same path
item.description: Can we investigate shade without a thermometer? Stand in a safe shaded spot, then a nearby sunny spot. Compare how comfortable each feels and discuss where more shade would help. Allow about 20 minutes. Try the shade and heat comparison.

media:content.media:description: A jacaranda casts a purple shadow across a sunlit path and grass.

item.title: Backyard wildlife shelter for kids using fallen garden materials
item.description: What can we use to make a tiny wildlife shelter? Start with loose fallen leaves, sticks, bark, stones or pine cones in your own yard. Leave occupied patches undisturbed and observe from a short distance. Get the free five-day Nature Tracker with an adult email.

media:content.media:description: A pine cone, two twigs, a fallen leaf and a smooth stone rest beside moss.

item.title: School garden biodiversity lesson: help children choose one action
item.description: How can children turn a habitat observation into action? At the end of Operation: Hidden Habitat, ask which patch showed more signs of life. Use what the group noticed to choose a realistic way to care for that spot, such as keeping feet on the path. Get the free Teacher Starter Pack with an adult email.

media:content.media:description: A timber rail and stone path border red kangaroo paws in a school garden.

item.title: Saltwater float experiment for kids: will the same grape float?
item.description: How can we see what salt changes? With a grown-up, test the same grape in fresh water and in salt water. Add salt gradually, stir until it dissolves and record what happens. Changing the water while keeping the grape the same makes the comparison useful. Try the free Saltwater Float Test.

media:content.media:description: Two clear glasses of water sit beside a green grape and a small bowl of salt.

item.title: Water-saving activity for kids: start with the garden tap
item.description: What water-saving job can a child try today? After watering, ask them to remind a grown-up to check the tap is turned off. It is one way to try the Earth Protector Test. A parent, guardian or teacher can sign up for more activities. Open the free mini missions.

media:content.media:description: A drop hangs from a brass garden tap beside orange nasturtiums.

item.title: Beach nature walk for kids: follow the last high tide line
item.description: What made the line of shells and seaweed on the beach? The last high tide left them behind. On a safe beach walk with a grown-up, follow the line parallel to the water and describe three natural finds. Leave them in place. Try the free Tide-Line Detective activity.

media:content.media:description: Shells, seaweed and driftwood form a curving line across sand beside turquoise water.

item.title: Backyard birdwatching for kids: observe visitors without feeding them
item.description: Should we put out food to see who visits our little habitat? The Nature Tracker asks families to observe without touching, trapping or feeding wildlife. Watch from a short distance and write down what the bird does on its own. Get the free tracker with an adult email.

media:content.media:description: A blue fairywren perches on a flowering shrub, seen through a round opening.

item.title: Beach sign activity for kids: explain one wildlife-safe action in eight words
item.description: Can a child design a sign people understand in five seconds? Pick one action, such as giving shorebirds space. Draw one clear picture and use no more than eight words. Show someone for five seconds and ask what they think the sign means. Try the free beach sign activity.

media:content.media:description: Coloured pencils and a blank sheet on a clipboard lie on a striped beach towel beside the sea.

item.title: Five-day nature journal for kids: keep a dated record of one little habitat
item.description: How can we tell which clues we saw on which visit? Return to the same little wildlife habitat over five days. Date each entry and record the weather, clues and visitors you notice. A parent, guardian or teacher can use an adult email to get the free Nature Tracker.

media:content.media:description: A grass parakeet perches over a row of five numbered circles, one for each visit to a small habitat.

item.title: Homeschool habitat study for kids exploring leaf litter
item.description: What can children spot without lifting a log? Look along the edge of a fallen branch for webs, tracks, holes or fungi. Ask what makes this patch a good home for a tiny creature. Try the free Micro-Habitat Detective activity.

media:content.media:description: A historic plate of mushrooms sits beside three clues to look for in leaf litter, with the official Earth Protectors logo below.
